segments.translit: tamevārthaṃ parārthāya karuṇāndolitacittena bhusukupādo hariṇāśabdasandhyābhāṣayā kathayati—
segments.translation: For the sake of others, with a [mind]{citta} stirred by [compassion]{karuna}, [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku} tells that same meaning in the [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa} of the word ‘[deer]{deer}’:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song as [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku}'s teaching, told for the sake of others by a mind stirred by compassion, and spoken ‘in the [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa} of the word deer’: the [deer]{deer} is a coded image, whose sense the rest of his comment discloses (cp.06.m1).

flags.note: tam evārthaṃ, ‘that same meaning’: probably the teaching Munidatta has been expounding in the songs before this one, though it could mean ‘this very meaning’, about to be set out. I chose ‘that same meaning’, which keeps the ambiguity.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) agrees in substance: de lta bu'i don, ‘such a meaning’, for tam evārthaṃ; sems snying rjes bskul ba, ‘mind urged on by compassion’, for karuṇāndolitacitta, ‘mind set swinging by compassion’; and dgongs pa'i skad, ‘intentional language’, for sandhyābhāṣā, the usual Tibetan rendering, which takes the word as sandhā, ‘intention’, rather than sandhyā, ‘twilight’.

segments.translit: kāheretyādi| anādikālamādāyāsaṃprajanyadoṣeṇa mṛtyumāraviṣāveṣṭitaḥ san māra mār[e]ti hākaṃ mama cittahariṇena śrutaṃ| idānīṃ gurucaraṇareṇuprabhāvāt taṃ vihāya sarvvadharmmānulambhatayā grāhyagrāhakābhāvatvāt kāpi gṛhī[11ka]tvā muktvā sthito'ham|
segments.translation: ‘Whom…’ and so on. From beginningless time, through the fault of lacking [vigilance]{samprajanya}, wrapped in the poison of the [Māra of death]{mrtyumara}, my [mind]{citta}-[deer]{deer} heard the cry ‘Kill! Kill!’ Now, by the power of the dust of the [guru]{guru}'s feet, I have left that behind: through the [non-apprehension]{anupalambha} of all [dharmas]{dharma}, [the grasped and the grasper]{grahya-grahaka} are absent, and so I remain, having taken up whatever it was and let it go.
segments.note: Munidatta hears couplet 1 in the poet's own voice: from beginningless time his mind-[deer]{deer}, poisoned by the [Māra of death]{mrtyumara} through lack of vigilance, heard the cry ‘Kill! Kill!’; now, by the guru's grace, finding neither grasped nor grasper, he remains, having taken and let go. The question becomes a statement. The Tibetan translation has him ‘remain free’ (cp.06.m2).

equations.en: the mind, which Munidatta calls 'the mind-deer' (cittahariṇa) throughout his comment

flags.note: sarvvadharmmānulambhatayā: anulambha is not a known word. I read anupalambha, ‘non-apprehension’, which the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) supports with dmigs su med pa, and translated accordingly.

māra mār[e]ti rests on Shastri's restored e; the Tibetan sod sod ces, ‘saying “kill, kill”’, confirms it. The cry māra, ‘kill!’, may also play on the Māra of death just named: that is my observation, not something Munidatta says. The lemma kāhera differs slightly from the song's kāhairi (cp.06.1a).

mṛtyumāraviṣāveṣṭitaḥ san is nominative, while the agent of the sentence is the instrumental mama cittahariṇena, ‘by my mind-deer’. The loose syntax leaves open whether the speaker or his mind-deer is ‘wrapped in the poison’; I attached it to the mind-deer.

kāpi gṛhītvā muktvā sthito'ham paraphrases song line 1a (kāhairi ghini meli acchahu) but turns its question into a statement. kāpi may be kā api, ‘whatever (it was)’, or kvāpi, ‘anywhere’; a lost negative (‘having taken and let go of nothing’) would suit ‘the grasped and the grasper are absent’ better. I kept the text as it stands: ‘having taken up whatever it was and let it go’.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) differs twice. It has rgol ba, ‘attackers’, where the Sanskrit has hākaṃ, ‘the cry’ (as in its own version of line 1b, mtha' skor rgol ba), so that the mind-deer hears attackers crying ‘kill, kill’. And it ends cis kyang bzung nas bdag nyid grol bar gnas pa'o, ‘having taken hold in whatever way, I myself remain free’, reading muktvā as ‘freed’ rather than ‘having let go’.
hākaṃ: Munidatta keeps the song's Old Bengali word hāka inside his Sanskrit, with a Sanskrit accusative ending. This supports the draft's ‘the cry’ in line 1b.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena dṛ[ḍha]yati—
apaṇetyādi ata evaṃ svayaṃ kṛtāvidyāmātsaryyadoṣeṇa cāñcalyatayā pu[na]ḥ sa eva cittahariṇaḥ (ṇāḥ) sarvveṣāṃ baddhavairī| kṣaṇamapi cittaṃ cittahariṇaṃ vihāya bhusukkupādā'kheṭikaḥ| sadguruvacanabāṇenānyaṃ praharati| tamevamiti|
tathāca bodhicaryyāvatāre—
imaṃ carmmapuṭaṃ tāvat svabuddhyaiva pṛthak kuru
asthipañjarato māṃsaṃ prajñāśastreṇa mocaya||
asthīnyapi pṛthak kṛtvā paśyajñānamanantataḥ
kimatra sāramastīti svayameva vicāraya||
segments.translation: With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he makes this firm: ‘Its own…’ and so on. So, in this way, through the fault of [ignorance]{avidya} and [avarice]{matsarya} that it has made itself, and through its restlessness, that same [mind]{citta}-[deer]{deer} is once more the sworn enemy of all. [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku}, the [hunter]{hunter}, does not let go of the [mind]{citta}, the [mind]{citta}-[deer]{deer}, even for a moment; with the arrow of the true [guru]{guru}'s words he strikes the other. Just so. And so the [Bodhicaryāvatāra]{tx-bodhicaryavatara} says: ‘First, with your own understanding, set apart this bag of skin; with the knife of [wisdom]{prajna}, free the flesh from the cage of bones. Then set the bones apart as well, and look at the marrow at the last. Examine it for yourself: what core is there in this?’
segments.note: Munidatta reads the refrain as confirming this: through its self-made faults of [ignorance]{avidya} and [avarice]{matsarya}, and its restlessness, the mind-deer is the sworn enemy of all. Bhusukupāda is the [hunter]{hunter}, striking ‘the other’ with the arrow of the true guru's words; verses from the Bodhicaryāvatāra on stripping the body follow. The Tibetan has Bhusuku's ‘examination’ for the hunter (cp.06.m3).

equations.en: Bhusukupāda himself, who strikes 'the other' with the arrow of the true guru's words (sadguruvacanavāṇa); the Tibetan has his 'examination' (sor rtog) and the arrow of the true guru's feet

citations.quoted: imaṃ carmmapuṭaṃ tāvat svabuddhyaiva pṛthak kuru / asthipañjarato māṃsaṃ prajñāśastreṇa mocaya // asthīnyapi pṛthak kṛtvā paśyajñānamanantataḥ / kimatra sāramastīti svayameva vicāraya
citations.work: Bodhicaryāvatāra (named by Munidatta); apparently chapter 5, on guarding vigilance, verses 62–63

flags.note: dṛ[ḍha]yati and pu[na]ḥ are Shastri's restorations; the Tibetan brtan par byed do, ‘makes firm’, confirms the first. Shastri's parenthesis cittahariṇaḥ (ṇāḥ) offers a plural; the singular suits sa eva and is kept.

kṣaṇam api cittaṃ cittahariṇaṃ vihāya has no negative: literally ‘leaving the mind, the mind-deer, even for a moment’. The song has khanaha na chāṛaa, ‘does not let go for a moment’, and kṣaṇam api needs a negative to make sense (perhaps read cittahariṇam avihāya). The Tibetan also lacks it (skad cig nyid kyang spong ba'o, ‘abandons even for a moment’), so the loss may be old. I translated with the negative.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) differs in several places: sems can, ‘sentient being’, for citta in ‘that same mind-deer’; thams cad kyi dgra yis bskor bas, ‘surrounded by the enemies of all’, for sarvveṣāṃ baddhavairī, ‘the sworn enemy of all’; sor rtog, ‘examination’, for ākheṭikaḥ, ‘the hunter’ (so also its line 2b, sor rtog skad cig mi 'dor); and bla ma dam pa'i zhabs kyi mda', ‘the arrow of the true guru's feet’, for sadguruvacanabāṇa, ‘the arrow of the true guru's words’, as if reading caraṇa for vacana.

anyaṃ praharati, ‘strikes the other’: who the other is is not said; perhaps the mind-deer, perhaps other beings. The Tibetan gzhan la 'phen pa, ‘shoots at another’, is equally open. anyaṃ could also be a slip for enaṃ, ‘it’.

tam evam iti is obscure: perhaps ‘just so’, closing the paraphrase (the Tibetan de lta bu nyid ces, ‘“just so”’, joins it to the quotation that follows), or a gloss taking ‘the other’ as ‘him’. I translated ‘Just so.’

In the Bodhicaryāvatāra verse the edition's paśyajñānamanantataḥ (‘see knowledge… endlessly’?) makes no sense. The known text of the verse reads paśya majjānam antataḥ, ‘look at the marrow at the last’, and the Tibetan rkang mar nang du bltas pa, ‘having looked inside at the marrow’, supports it. I translated ‘marrow’.
Munidatta's mātsarya, ‘avarice’, where the song has māṃsa, ‘flesh’, may be a sound-echo; he does not say so, and the note does not claim it.

segments.translit:
cittahariṇasya niḥsaṃśayaṃ pratipādanāya āha—
tiṇa na khaṇḍai ityādi| yathā bāhyairmṛgaiḥ tṛṇacchedanirjharapānaṃ kriyate tadvat cittahariṇanna karoti| viśiṣya vicārasvarūpeṇa tayoḥ cittapavanayoḥ nilayaṃ nivāsa indriyadvāreṇa nāvagamyate|
tathāca kṛṣṇācāryyapādairabhihitaṃ dohākoṣe—
varagiriśihara utuṅga thali śaba[12]rehiṃ kiavāsa|
nau laṃghiya pañcānanauhaṃ karivara dūri nivāsa||
segments.translation: To establish the [mind]{citta}-[deer]{deer} beyond doubt, he says: ‘It does not crop the grass…’ and so on. Outer [deer]{deer} crop grass and drink from mountain streams; the [mind]{citta}-[deer]{deer} does not do so. Considered more closely, in its [true nature]{svarupa} as analysis shows it, the lair, that is, the [dwelling]{nivasa}, of those two, [mind]{citta} and [wind]{vayu}, is not understood through the door of the [senses]{indriya}. And so [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} has said in the [Dohākoṣa]{tx-dohakosa}: ‘On the high ground of the great mountain's lofty peak the [Śabaras]{sabara} have made their home. Lions do not leap to it; the great [elephant]{elephant} has its [dwelling]{nivasa} far away.’
segments.note: Munidatta reads couplet 3 as proving the mind-deer: unlike outer deer, it neither crops grass nor drinks from streams (his text of the line has ‘crop’, khaṇḍai, for ‘touch’). The unknown dwelling is that of ‘those two, mind and [wind]{vayu}’, which the senses cannot reach; he does not say which animal is which. A dohā of Kāṇha follows (cp.06.m4).

equations.en: the mind, which Munidatta calls 'the mind-deer' (cittahariṇa) throughout his comment

citations.quoted: varagiriśihara utuṅga thali śabarehiṃ kiavāsa / nau laṃghiya pañcānanauhaṃ karivara dūri nivāsa
citations.work: Dohākoṣa of Kṛṣṇācārya (Kāṇha), named by Munidatta

flags.note: Munidatta's lemma reads tiṇa na khaṇḍai, ‘does not crop (break) the grass’, where the song (cp.06.3a) has tiṇa na cchupai, ‘does not touch’; his paraphrase tṛṇaccheda, ‘cropping grass’, shows the lemma is not a slip. The Tibetan commentary's lemma likewise differs from its own song line: rtswa mi za, ‘does not eat grass’, against rtswa la mi reg, ‘does not touch grass’.

viśiṣya vicārasvarūpeṇa is hard to construe: ‘specifically, by the true nature of analysis’, or ‘examined as to its true nature’. The Tibetan khyad par du rnam par dpyod pa'i rang bzhin gyis is just as literal. I translated ‘considered more closely, in its true nature as analysis shows it’.

tayoḥ cittapavanayoḥ, ‘of those two, mind and wind’, stands where the song has hariṇā hariṇira, ‘of the deer and the doe’. It is a paraphrase, not an explicit gloss, and it does not say which animal is which; word order would make the deer the mind and the doe the wind, but in the next segment the doe is the jñānamudrā (cp.06.m5).

Munidatta glosses the song's nilaa as nilaya, ‘that is, nivāsa’. The draft renders nilaa ‘dwelling’, and the glossary's nivasa term is also ‘dwelling’, so I gave nilaya as ‘lair’ to keep the gloss visible; the reviewer may prefer ‘the dwelling (nilaya), that is, the abode’.
cittahariṇan na karoti: the subject stands in an accusative or neuter form (cittahariṇam) rather than the nominative; the sense is clear.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) renders the dohā differently: ri mchog rtse mo mthong ba yi / thang la sha ba ri dgas bcas, ‘on the plain of the best mountain's peak, seen (mthong ba, probably for mtho ba, ‘high’), are stags and deer’, taking śabarehiṃ as sha ba, ‘stag’, rather than the Śabara people. Its last lines agree: gdong lnga pa, ‘the lion’, does not leap; glang chen mchog, ‘the best of elephants’, dwells far. In the opening sentence it has rtogs pa, ‘realizing’, for pratipādana, ‘establishing’.

The dohā's Apabhraṃśa is only partly clear. I take nau as ṇa u, ‘not’; pañcānanauhaṃ as an instrumental plural, ‘by lions’ (pañcānana, ‘five-faced’, the lion); laṃghiya as ‘leapt over, reached’; and kiavāsa as kia vāsa, ‘made (their) home’.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena kāyapavanaviṣayapallavopasaṃhāramāha—
hariṇītyādi| viṣapānabhavagrahān (ṇa) harati khaṇḍayati| hariṇīti sandhyābhāṣayā saiva jñānamudrā nairātmā bhāvakasyābhyāsaprakarṣavaśāt āśvāsaṃ bho cittahariṇa asya kāyavanasya kāyagrahaṃ vihāya ṣanmahāsukhakamalavanaṃ gatvā vibhrāntivikalpaiścacāra(raḥ)|
tathāca sahajasaṃvare—
sarvvavyāpi nirābhāṣi karuṇaikarasaṃ manaḥ|
āliṅgati jhaṭityeṣā vṛṣasyantī ca śūnyatā||
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he speaks of the withdrawal of the shoots of body, [wind]{vayu} and [sense objects]{visaya}: ‘The [doe]{doe}…’ and so on. She takes away (harati), that is, cuts off, the graspings at [existence]{bhava} that are a drinking of poison. ‘Doe’ (hariṇī): in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa} she is that very [jñānamudrā]{jnanamudra}, [Nairātmā]{nairatma}. By the force of the meditator's heightened practice she gives comfort: ‘O [mind]{citta}-[deer]{deer}, give up your grasping at the body in this body-[forest]{forest}, go to the [lotus]{lotus} grove of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, and roam with deluded [conceptual thought]{vikalpa}.’ And so the [Sahajasaṃvara]{tx-sahajasamvara} says: ‘This [emptiness]{sunyata}, a woman burning with desire, at once embraces the [mind]{citta} that is all-pervading, free of [appearance]{abhasa}, of [one taste]{ekarasa} with [compassion]{karuna}.’
segments.note: Munidatta calls the [doe]{doe} twilight language for the wisdom seal ([jñānamudrā]{jnanamudra}), Nairātmā, who ‘takes away’ (harati) the graspings of existence. As the meditator's practice matures she comforts the mind-deer: leave the grasping at the body, this body-[forest]{forest}, for the lotus grove of great bliss. Where his Sanskrit ends ‘with deluded concepts’, the Tibetan has ‘free of’ them (cp.06.m5).

equations.en: the wisdom seal (jñānamudrā), Nairātmā: hariṇī is twilight language for her, 'she who takes away' (harati) the graspings of existence; as the meditator's practice matures she comforts the mind-deer and tells it to leave the body-forest for the lotus grove of great bliss
the body, 'this body-forest' (kāyavana): the mind-deer is to give up its grasping at the body (kāyagraha) and go to the lotus grove of great bliss

citations.quoted: sarvvavyāpi nirābhāṣi karuṇaikarasaṃ manaḥ / āliṅgati jhaṭityeṣā vṛṣasyantī ca śūnyatā
citations.work: Sahajasaṃvara (named by Munidatta; not otherwise identified here)

flags.note: kāyapavana-, ‘body and wind’: the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has lus kyi nags, ‘the forest of the body’, that is kāyavana, the word Munidatta uses a few lines later; its heading reads ‘the gathering in of the stirring of the leaves (lo ma g.yo ba) in the domain of the body-forest’. kāyavana may be the better reading; I translated the Sanskrit as printed.

kāyapavanaviṣayapallavopasaṃhāra can be divided several ways: ‘the withdrawal of the shoots of body, wind and sense objects’ (my choice); ‘the withdrawal of the shoots, the sense objects, of body and wind’; or, with the Tibetan's kāyavana, ‘the withdrawal of the leaves, the sense objects, of the body-forest’. upasaṃhāra can also mean ‘conclusion’.

viṣapāna-, ‘drinking of poison’: the Tibetan has yul gyi chu, ‘the water of sense objects’, that is viṣaya for viṣa, which suits a deer that drinks no water (cp.06.3a). It explains the name with 'gog pa, ‘stopping’, and cannot reproduce the play on hariṇī and harati, ‘takes away’.
grahān (ṇa): Shastri's parenthesis seems to suggest grahaṇa, ‘grasping’; the sense is unchanged.

āśvāsaṃ, ‘comfort’, has no verb. The Tibetan supplies one (dbugs 'byin pa ster bar byed, ‘gives comfort’) and takes -vaśāt, ‘by the force of’, as dbang du 'gugs, ‘brings under her power’. I translated ‘she gives comfort’.
kāyagrahaṃ, ‘grasping at the body’: the Tibetan has lus kyi khyim, ‘the house of the body’, that is kāyagṛha.

ṣanmahāsukha…: ṣan gives no sense. I read yan (yat), Bengali ষ and য being easily confused; the Tibetan gang la, ‘to which’, supports a relative pronoun. The sense, ‘go to the lotus grove of great bliss’, is unaffected.

vibhrāntivikalpaiś cacāra(raḥ): as printed, ‘roamed with deluded conceptual thought’. cacāra is a third-person perfect where the doe's speech needs an imperative (cara), and ‘with deluded concepts’ runs against the context. The Tibetan has 'khrul pa'i rnam par rtog pa med pa la spyod do, ‘roam where there is no deluded conceptual thought’, which probably keeps the intended sense (a privative, or vinā, may be lost). Another possibility: vibhrānti-vikalpa as ‘wanderings of every kind’, glossing the song's bhānto. I translated the Sanskrit literally; the reviewer should decide.

In the Sahajasaṃvara verse the Tibetan has dmigs med, ‘without object’, for nirābhāṣi, ‘free of appearance’; renders vṛṣasyantī ca as 'dod ldan ma bzhin du, ‘like a woman in desire’ (as if iva for ca); and turns the verse into an instruction (‘the mind of one taste with compassion … like a woman in desire, embrace emptiness at once’), so that the mind embraces emptiness rather than emptiness the mind.
nirābhāṣi is read nirābhāsi, ‘free of appearance’ (ṣ written for s).

segments.translit:
caturthapadenādhimātrādhimātrasyānuśaṃsāmāha—
taraṃgate hariṇā ityādi| sahajajñānāvabodhena yoginastasya svacittahariṇasyāvayavādi—vikalpaṃ na kalpayanti| ye'pi bahiḥśāstrāgamābhimāninaḥ paṇḍitāste'pyasmin dharmme saṃmūḍhā dūratarāḥ| bhusukupādasiddhācāryyo hi vadati teṣāṃ hṛdaye kiñcit tatvonmīli(la)tamātraṃ na bhavatīti| yaduktaṃ [12ka] bhagavatā caturdevīparipṛcchāmahāyogatantre|
caturāśītisāhasraṃ dharmmaskandhe muneḥ + +|
tattvaṃ ye na [hi] jānanti te sarvve(rvva) niṣphalāya vai|| 6||
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he speaks in [praise]{anusamsa} of the practitioner of the very highest capacity: ‘As it bounds, the [deer]{deer}…’ and so on. Through realizing [innate]{sahaja} knowledge, [yogis]{yogi} form no [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} about the parts and so on of that, their own [mind]{citta}-[deer]{deer}. Even those scholars who pride themselves on outer treatises and scriptures are thoroughly deluded about this [dharma]{dharma} and very far from it. For the [siddha]{siddha} master [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku} says that in their hearts not even the least opening onto [reality]{tattva} takes place. As the [Blessed One]{p-bhagavat} said in the mahāyoga tantra [Caturdevīparipṛcchā]{tx-caturdevipariprccha}: ‘The Sage's eighty-four thousand [heaps of Dharma]{dharmaskandha}… for those who do not know [reality]{tattva}, all of them are fruitless.’
segments.note: Munidatta takes the last couplet as praise of the most capable practitioner: yogis who realize innate knowledge form no concepts of the parts of their mind-deer, in place of the song's unseen hooves. The [fools]{mudha} are scholars proud of outer treatises, deluded about this teaching, in whom reality never opens. The Tibetan praises ‘small, great and so on’ (cp.06.m6).

equations.en: scholars (paṇḍita) proud of outer treatises and scriptures, thoroughly deluded about this teaching and far from it, in whose hearts not even a glimmer of reality opens

citations.quoted: caturāśītisāhasraṃ dharmmaskandhe muneḥ + + / tattvaṃ ye na [hi] jānanti te sarvve(rvva) niṣphalāya vai
citations.work: Caturdevīparipṛcchā, a mahāyoga tantra, named by Munidatta

flags.note: adhimātrādhimātra-, ‘of the very highest degree’: the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has chung ngu dang chen po la sogs pa, ‘small, great and so on’, so that the fourth verse praises practitioners of every grade, not only the highest.

adhimātrādhimātra is the top of the ninefold scale of Buddhist scholastics (mild, middling, strong, each subdivided), usually applied to faculties or capacities. ‘The practitioner of the very highest capacity’ supplies the noun Munidatta leaves implicit.

yoginas tasya svacittahariṇasya: yoginas may be nominative plural, ‘yogis’, agreeing with the plural verb kalpayanti (my choice), or genitive singular with tasya, ‘of that yogi's own mind-deer’, as the Tibetan takes it (rnal 'byor pa de'i rang gi sems kyi ri dgas).

avayavādi, ‘the parts and so on’, stands where the song has khūra, ‘hooves’ (cp.06.5a). Munidatta gives no explicit gloss of the hooves or of taraṅgante, ‘as it bounds’; his lemma reads taraṃgate hariṇā for the song's taraṅgante hariṇāra.

tatvonmīli(la)ta-: Shastri marks the word as doubtful, but the sense, ‘opening (of the eyes)’, is clear. The Tibetan has mig nye bar zhi ba, ‘the eye quite stilled’, apparently reading or understanding the word differently (nimīlita, ‘closed’?).

In the tantra verse two syllables are lost after muneḥ, ‘of the Sage’; the Tibetan thub chen, ‘the great Sage’, does not fill them. te sarvve(rvva) niṣphalāya vai is irregular (a dative, ‘for fruitlessness’), but the sense ‘all are fruitless’ is clear. The Tibetan's last line, de rnams thams cad 'bral med yin, ‘all of them are inseparable’, looks like a slip for 'bras med, ‘fruitless’.
saṃmūḍhā, ‘thoroughly deluded’, picks up the song's mūṛhā, ‘fools’ (cp.06.5b); I did not force the glossary's ‘fool’ onto the participle; the note marks the song's ‘fools’ instead.

proposals.definition: Praise, or the benefit of a practice (anuśaṃsā): Munidatta's word for what a song's closing couplet sets out. Here he says the fourth verse speaks in praise of the practitioner of the very highest capacity (cp.06.m6); the Tibetan has rjes su bsngags pa, ‘praise’.
proposals.rationale: A structural word in Munidatta's introductions to closing couplets. It recurs: the glossary's yoginī forms include yoginyānuśaṃsām āha from another song. Buddhist Sanskrit anuśaṃsā usually means ‘benefit, advantage’, while the Tibetan here takes it as ‘praise’, so one rendering should be fixed.

questions: cp.06.3a: Munidatta's lemma (cp.06.m4) reads tiṇa na khaṇḍai, ‘does not crop the grass’, and his paraphrase agrees; the song text has cchupai, ‘touches’, and the Tibetan commentary's lemma has ‘eat’. Should the draft of 3a carry a witness note?

cp.06.m3: both the Sanskrit and the Tibetan lack the negative that the refrain has (na chāṛaa), so the text literally says ‘leaving … even for a moment’. I translated ‘does not let go … even for a moment’. Do you accept supplying the negative, or prefer the literal text with a note?

cp.06.m5: vibhrāntivikalpaiś cacāra reads literally ‘roam(ed) with deluded conceptual thought’, while the Tibetan has ‘free of’ it. I kept the literal Sanskrit and flagged it high. Would you rather print the Tibetan's sense and note the Sanskrit?

cp.06.m3: the Bodhicaryāvatāra verse's paśyajñānamanantataḥ is corrupt. I translated the known reading paśya majjānam antataḥ (‘marrow’), which the Tibetan supports. Is it acceptable to emend a quotation on that basis?

p-kanha: Munidatta names the author of the Dohākoṣa as Kṛṣṇācāryapāda (cp.06.m4), but the approved English is Kāṇha, which I used. In commentary translations, should his Sanskrit name form be kept, perhaps as a listed variant?

vikalpa: the approved ‘conceptual thought’ reads stiffly in ‘form no conceptual thought about the parts…’ (cp.06.m6) and ‘roam with deluded conceptual thought’ (cp.06.m5). Could ‘concepts’ be added as a variant?

keep-source-first-gloss terms first met in this commentary (jñānamudrā and Nairātmā in cp.06.m5, Śabara in cp.06.m4, siddha in cp.06.m6): the weave schema has no separate notes, so I relied on the glossary links and glossed jñānamudrā in the cp.06.m5 note. Is that enough?
Proposal anusamsa: ‘praise’ follows the Tibetan rjes su bsngags pa here; ‘benefit’ is the usual Buddhist Sanskrit sense. Which should the edition use?
